commitResults.messageTitle: Level 7: save and load the task list
commitResults.messageBody:
Until now the task list existed only in memory, so closing the program
threw away everything the user had entered.

Add a Storage class that owns all file handling: it writes the list to
./data/goat.txt after every change and reads it back at start-up.
Keeping this in one class means the rest of Goat never has to know where
the data lives or how it is encoded.

Encoding is split the same way toString() already is. Task supplies the
shared "1 | description" half of a line, and each subclass prepends its
type letter and appends its own fields, so adding a task type later
means touching only that class. Decoding is centralised in
Storage.parseTask, which is the exact inverse. The done status is stored
as 1/0 rather than the X shown on screen, so the display wording can
change without invalidating files people have already saved.

Saving happens before the confirmation message is printed, so the user
is never told about a change that did not actually reach the disk.
Storage throws GoatException, which the existing catch around the
command dispatch already reports, so no new error handling was needed.

The app has to work on someone else's computer, so:
- the path is built with Paths.get("data", "goat.txt"), which is
  relative and lets Java insert whichever separator the running system
  uses, instead of baking in a "/" that would be wrong on Windows
- a missing file is not an error, since that is the normal state on a
  first run
- a missing ./data folder is created by Files.createDirectories
- a hand-edited file with a mistake in it names the offending line and
  starts with an empty list rather than crashing

Restore the text-ui-test harness and extend it to four runs of the
program: one that adds, marks and deletes; one that only lists, proving
the tasks came back from disk; one that reads a deliberately damaged
file; and one that starts with the save file deleted but the folder left
in place. The runner clears ./data first, because a leftover file would
be loaded at start-up and the test would stop being repeatable. Also
replace dos2unix with a tr fallback, as dos2unix is not installed on
macOS by default.

Ignore data/, since the saved list is personal to whoever runs the app,
and rename the remaining Duke references to Goat in README.md,
docs/README.md and AGENTS.md.

Deadlines and events kept whatever text the user typed, so "Sunday" and
"2/12/2019 1800" were just strings: Goat could echo them back but could
not compare two of them, sort by them, or reprint them in a nicer form.

Store them as java.time.LocalDateTime instead. Deadline.by and
Event.from/to change type, and the text is converted at the two edges
where it enters the program - Goat.createTask for typed input and
Storage.parseTask for a saved line - so a task object can never hold a
date that was never understood.

Put all three conversions in a new DateTimes class, because they have to
agree with one another: whatever toFileFormat writes, parse must read
back. Keeping them together means no task class contains a date pattern
and a format change touches one file.

Input accepts yyyy-MM-dd, with an optional time as yyyy-MM-dd HHmm; the
presence of a space is what tells the two apart. A date given without a
time is stored at midnight, which is also how it is later recognised as
"no time given" and printed as just a date. That is a simplification - a
task genuinely due at 00:00 prints without a time - but a separate
boolean or a second field of type LocalDate is more state than a task
list needs.

Output uses MMM dd yyyy ("Oct 15 2019"), with ", h:mm" and a lowercase
am/pm appended when a time is present ("Dec 02 2019, 6:00pm"). The
am/pm wording comes from a DateTimeFormatterBuilder rather than the
pattern letter "a", since "PM" shouts mid-sentence and lowercasing the
finished string would drag the month name down with it. Every formatter
is given Locale.ENGLISH explicitly, so month names do not change with
the machine the program runs on.

Save files write the time even when it is midnight, so one pattern reads
every line, and in the same format the user types, so a file edited by
hand uses a syntax they already know. Note that this invalidates files
saved by earlier versions: a line such as "D | 0 | return book | June
6th" is now reported as a damaged line rather than loaded.

Unreadable dates raise GoatException with the accepted formats spelled
out, since java.time's own message names the character it stopped at,
which does not help someone who simply used another format. The existing
catch around the command dispatch reports it, so a bad date does not end
the session.

Update the text-ui-test inputs to the new format and extend the first
run with a rejected date ("next Friday") and a date without a time. The
damaged-file run now uses a badly formatted date instead of an unknown
task type, as that is the easier mistake to make by hand and it proves
dates are validated on loading too.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract Ui class for all user interaction
commitResults.messageBody:
Goat mixed three unrelated jobs in one class: formatting and printing
replies, reading the user's input, and deciding what each command means.
The first two are a single concern -- talking to the user -- and they are
the easiest to separate cleanly, so they go first.

Ui now owns the divider, the indent, the "OOPS!!! " prefix, the start-up
banner and the Scanner, and exposes named messages (showWelcome,
showGoodbye, showError, showLoadingError) plus a general show(String...).
Goat no longer refers to System.out or System.in at all.

Ui is instance-based rather than static like Storage, because it owns a
Scanner that has to be created and closed; an object is the natural home
for something with a lifetime. The handler methods take the Ui as a
parameter for now, which keeps this commit to the extraction alone; they
will lose that parameter when Goat itself becomes an object holding ui,
tasks and storage as fields.

Behaviour is unchanged: text-ui-test passes byte-for-byte against
EXPECTED.TXT across all four runs (fresh start, restart, damaged save
file, deleted save file).

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract TaskList class to own the task list
commitResults.messageBody:
Goat previously passed a bare ArrayList<Task> to every helper method.
The list had no behaviour of its own, so the rules about it were spread
across whichever helper happened to be running: each of setDone() and
deleteTask() repeated the same "is this a real task number?" check, and
each repeated the conversion from the 1-based number the user types to
the 0-based index the ArrayList uses.

TaskList now wraps the list and exposes add/delete/get/size/isEmpty.
The wrapped ArrayList is private and is never handed out, and the
constructor copies the list it is given, so tasks can only be added or
removed through those methods. get() and delete() take the task number
as the user counts it and do the range check themselves, which removes
the duplicated check and puts the off-by-one in exactly one place
(the private toIndex()).

Goat keeps only the string-to-int step, as parseTaskNumber(String); it
belongs with the command parsing that a later increment will extract,
not with the list. Storage.save() now takes a TaskList and walks it by
number instead of with a for-each, since TaskList deliberately does not
expose its ArrayList.

No behaviour change: text-ui-test passes unchanged, and the messages for
a non-numeric, out-of-range, zero or missing task number are the same as
before.

commitResults.messageTitle: Rename the Command enum to CommandType
commitResults.messageBody:
A pure rename, committed on its own so it does not hide inside the next
change.

The enum's constants only identify which command was typed; they carry
none of the work of executing it. Calling the enum "Command" therefore
claims a name it does not earn, and it claims the name the stretch goal
of this increment wants for the *Command classes (AddCommand,
DeleteCommand, ExitCommand) that will do that work. Renaming now costs
one commit; renaming later would mean rewriting the classes that had
already been built against the old name.

No behaviour change: text-ui-test passes unchanged.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract Parser class for reading the user's input
commitResults.messageBody:
Goat was both reading the user's text and acting on it in the same
methods. createTask() in particular was 40 lines of splitting on "/by",
"/from" and "/to" sitting in the middle of a class whose job is meant to
be dispatch, which meant a change to how a command is *written* landed in
the same method that adds tasks and saves files.

Parser now owns every step that turns text into a value:
  parseCommandType()  first word -> CommandType
  parseArgument()     the rest of the line
  parseTaskNumber()   "3" -> 3
  parseNewTask()      "return book /by 2019-12-02 1800" -> Deadline
The three "/..." markers are named constants, so the wording of a command
is stated once. createTask() moved here and split into parseTodo,
parseDeadline and parseEvent, one small method per format rather than one
switch with three inline blocks.

Because Parser only reads strings -- it never touches the list, the
screen or the disk -- each method can be tested by passing a string and
checking what comes back. That is what the later A-JUnit increment wants.

One check deliberately stayed behind in Goat: the complaint about a task
number left out entirely ("give a number for deleting"). It names the
command it came from, and only the caller knows that, so pushing it into
Parser would have cost the distinct wording for mark/unmark vs delete.

Goat is now 145 lines, down from 245 before this increment began, and
holds only the dispatch switch and the four handlers.

No behaviour change: text-ui-test passes, and all ten error messages
(bad/missing task number, missing description, missing dates, unknown
command) were checked by hand and are unchanged.

commitResults.messageTitle: Make Goat an object instead of one long static main
commitResults.messageBody:
Goat was a static main() with five static helpers, and every helper took
ui and tasks as parameters because static methods have nothing else to
read them from. Those two things last for the whole run and are used by
every handler, which is exactly the situation fields exist for.

Goat now holds ui and tasks as final fields, set up by a constructor;
run() drives the loop; main() is one line, "new Goat().run()". The five
handlers lose their ui/tasks parameters and become instance methods, so
their signatures now show only what actually varies per command.

Loading moved into the constructor, on the grounds that a Goat that has
not read its tasks is not ready to be used, and a constructor is the one
method guaranteed to run before anything else can. tasks is assigned via
a local because a final field cannot be set twice and the catch clause
needs a second go at deciding what it holds.

That move reordered the output at first: the constructor's loading
complaint appeared before run() had shown the welcome, which the
"damaged save file" run of text-ui-test caught. Greeting is now the
constructor's first act, before the load is attempted, so a complaint
about the save file is never the first thing the user sees.

text-ui-test passes.

commitResults.messageTitle: Make Storage an object that knows its own save file
commitResults.messageBody:
Storage was static, with the path baked in as a private constant. That
meant Storage decided where every task list in the program lives, and
nothing outside it could say otherwise -- including a test, which had no
way to point it at a scratch file instead of the user's real one.

Storage now takes the path in its constructor and keeps it in a field,
and load()/save() are instance methods. Goat holds one Storage as a
field alongside ui and tasks, and main() names the path:

    new Goat("data/goat.txt").run()

so the location of the save file is stated once, at the outermost edge
of the program, and no class below that line decides it.

The path is built with a plain Paths.get(filePath) rather than from
separate name parts, because Java's file classes accept "/" on every
operating system, Windows included.

This completes the minimal target of A-MoreOOP: Ui, Storage, Parser and
TaskList all exist, and Goat is down to dispatch plus four handlers.

text-ui-test passes.

First half of the A-MoreOOP stretch goal, committed on its own: these six
files are new and nothing calls them yet, so the commit that wires them
in stays readable.

Command is abstract, with an abstract execute(tasks, ui, storage) and an
isExit() that defaults to false. The five subclasses each hold the data
their own command needs and nothing more:

  AddCommand     a finished Task, built by Parser
  DeleteCommand  a task number
  MarkCommand    a task number and the status to set
  ListCommand    nothing
  ExitCommand    nothing

The bodies are the four private handlers lifted out of Goat, unchanged
apart from taking their collaborators as parameters instead of reading
fields.

Two design notes worth recording:

- The collaborators are parameters, not fields. A command is a
  short-lived description of one instruction -- built, run once,
  discarded -- and passing them in states plainly that a command may not
  reach for anything else.

- "mark" and "unmark" share MarkCommand rather than being two classes.
  They differ only in the status stored and one line of wording; the
  find-save-confirm skeleton is identical, so two classes would duplicate
  it to express a single differing value. If they ever grew genuinely
  different behaviour, they would become two subclasses of a shared
  parent and the boolean would disappear.

ExitCommand.execute() is deliberately empty: the farewell is owed whether
the user typed "bye" or the input ran out, so Goat keeps showing it once
after the loop.

commitResults.messageTitle: Dispatch through Command objects instead of a switch in Goat
commitResults.messageBody:
Second half of the stretch goal: wire in the Command classes added by the
previous commit.

Parser gains parse(String), which reads the line and returns the Command
it asks for. The switch that used to sit in Goat moved here, which is
where it belongs -- choosing a class based on a keyword is a parsing
decision, not a running-the-program one. It is also the last switch on
CommandType in the codebase; every other branch on "which command is
this?" is now handled by which subclass was built.

With parse() in place, four of Parser's methods stopped being part of its
public surface: parseCommandType, parseArgument, parseTaskNumber and
parseNewTask are steps in getting to a Command, and nothing outside
Parser has any reason to call them. They are now private.

The two "you left out the task number" messages moved from Goat into a
new private parseTaskNumberFor(), which picks the wording from the
CommandType. That was the one piece of command-specific knowledge still
stranded in Goat.

Goat is now 95 lines, down from 245 at the start of A-MoreOOP, and its
run loop is six lines:

    while (!isExit && ui.hasNextCommand()) {
        String fullCommand = ui.readCommand();
        try {
            Command command = Parser.parse(fullCommand);
            command.execute(tasks, ui, storage);
            isExit = command.isExit();
        } catch (GoatException e) {
            ui.showError(e.getMessage());
        }
    }

It no longer names a single command anywhere. Adding one means writing a
Command subclass and naming it in Parser.parse; Goat does not change.

Two deliberate departures from the shape given in the brief:

- The loop also tests ui.hasNextCommand(), because commands can be piped
  in from a file that ends without a "bye".
- There is no ui.showLine() / finally pair. Ui.show() already brackets
  every reply in dividers, so the layout of a reply stays in one place
  instead of being half here and half there.

No behaviour change: text-ui-test passes, and all eleven error messages
plus the list/mark/unmark replies were checked by hand and are unchanged.

commitResults.messageTitle: Organise the classes into packages under goat
commitResults.messageBody:
All 18 classes were in the default package, which meant every class could
see every other one and the four responsibilities established by
A-MoreOOP were a fact about the code rather than a fact about its
structure. They are now packages:

    goat            Goat, GoatException
    goat.command    Command + the five subclasses
    goat.task       Task, Todo, Deadline, Event, TaskList
    goat.parser     Parser, CommandType, DateTimes
    goat.storage    Storage
    goat.ui         Ui

src/main/java stays the source root; src, main and java are not packages.
Every file moved with git mv, so history follows each one.

GoatException sits at the root rather than in a package of its own,
because it is thrown across all five of the others and belongs to none.

No class needed widening to make this compile -- everything the packages
now have to share was already public. Javadoc links that cross a package
boundary without a matching import are written out in full (for example
{@link goat.task.TaskList} in Parser) rather than importing a class the
code never uses.

One stale comment fixed while moving: Ui's class doc said it was
instance-based "unlike Storage", which stopped being true when Storage
gained a filePath field. It now notes instead that Ui is the only class
allowed to touch System.out and System.in -- a rule the package structure
makes visible.

The test scripts had to change in the same commit, since they hard-coded
the flat layout:
- sources are gathered recursively (find on Unix, dir /s /b on Windows)
  instead of a single *.java wildcard;
- the main class is named goat.Goat;
- the source root is no longer put on javac's classpath, where stale
  .class files sitting next to the sources could shadow a fresh build.
In runtest.bat the errorlevel check now runs before sources.txt is
deleted, because del resets errorlevel and a build failure would
otherwise go unreported.

text-ui-test passes, and the error messages were spot-checked by hand.

commitResults.messageTitle: Hide CommandType inside the parser package
commitResults.messageBody:
A tightening the packaging just made possible, kept separate from the
move itself.

CommandType was public because everything was public when there was only
one package. Now that there are six, it turns out every use of the enum
is inside Parser, and all of them are in private methods: parse() reads
a keyword into a CommandType and immediately turns it into a Command, so
the enum never crosses the package boundary.

The enum and fromKeyword() are therefore package-private. Which keyword
a user typed is a detail of how a line gets read, and no other package
has any business knowing that an enum is how the reading is done.

The only references from outside were two Javadoc links in Command, which
could no longer resolve to a class they cannot see. Both now describe the
enum in prose instead, which reads better anyway: the point being made
there is about the division of labour, not about the type's name.

text-ui-test passes.

commitResults.messageTitle: Point the Gradle build at goat.Goat
commitResults.messageBody:
The build.gradle that came with add-gradle-support is written for the
template's chatbot, seedu.duke.Duke, which this project no longer has.
Three settings now name this project instead:

- application.mainClass is goat.Goat, so both `gradlew run` and the
  manifest Gradle writes into the JAR start the right class.
- shadowJar.archiveFileName is goat.jar rather than duke.jar.
- run.standardInput keeps its existing value, but with a comment: Gradle
  gives a run task no standard input by default, so without it Ui's
  Scanner would see the input end immediately and Goat would greet, say
  goodbye and quit without reading a single command.

Everything else is left as the branch supplied it. The JUnit 5 and shadow
plugin settings are already there and are used by the next two
increments; touching them now would be guessing ahead of those.

Verified with Gradle 9.6.1 on Java 25:
- `gradlew build` succeeds;
- `gradlew run` reads piped commands and replies as expected;
- `java -jar build/libs/goat.jar` runs standalone in an empty folder and
  writes its data/goat.txt there;
- text-ui-test still passes, so the javac-based path is unaffected.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add JUnit tests for the parsing, list, storage and command logic
commitResults.messageBody:
149 tests across 11 classes, run with `gradlew test` (and by `gradlew
build`). Test sources mirror the package of the class under test, and
method names follow featureUnderTest_testScenario_expectedBehavior.

What is covered, and why these first:

  DateTimesTest      Both edges where text becomes data. Every date a user
                     types and every date in the save file goes through
                     parse/format/toFileFormat, and a mistake either
                     rejects valid input or silently stores the wrong
                     moment. Includes 2019-02-29 vs 2020-02-29, the
                     midnight convention that means "no time given", and
                     a parse/write round trip.
  TaskListTest       The 1-based numbering and the range check that used
                     to be copied into each command handler. Also pins
                     the constructor's defensive copy, and that get()
                     hands back the live task rather than a copy.
  StorageTest        The save-file format, with the damaged-file cases
                     weighted most heavily: the file is plain text and a
                     user may edit it by hand, so Goat has to name the
                     faulty line rather than crash or lose the rest.
                     Uses JUnit's @TempDir, which is only possible
                     because Storage takes its path as an argument.
  ParserTest         The widest method in the program. Every keyword,
                     every way an argument can be missing or malformed,
                     and the exact wording of the complaints, since that
                     is what a user sees. A few tests execute the parsed
                     command, which is the only way to check it was built
                     around the right values.
  CommandTest        What each command does when it runs: the list ends
                     up right, the change reached the disk, and the user
                     was told. A command that quietly succeeds is as much
                     a bug as one that quietly fails.
  CommandTypeTest    The single place unrecognised input is rejected.
                     Checks the match is exact -- not by prefix, not
                     ignoring case -- since anything looser would accept
                     typos as commands.
  UiTest             The exact layout of a reply. text-ui-test compares
                     whole output byte for byte, so a stray space fails
                     it with a diff that takes a while to read; these
                     fail immediately and say which part is wrong.
  Task/Todo/Deadline/EventTest
                     The two renderings each task type owes, which differ
                     on purpose: the screen drops a midnight time, the
                     file always keeps one.

CommandTypeTest sits in goat.parser because the enum is package-private
after A-Packages; a test in the same package can still reach it, which is
the usual arrangement for something deliberately not part of a public
interface.

Tests that need Ui capture System.out and restore it afterwards, and
those that touch the disk write inside a per-test @TempDir, so no test
touches the real data/goat.txt.

AGENTS.md records the conventions and a coverage target of the top ~50%
highest-value methods, with a note that tests are to be updated in the
same change as the code rather than afterwards.

No production code changed. gradlew build passes and text-ui-test still
passes.

commitResults.messageTitle: Document building and distributing the goat.jar
commitResults.messageBody:
A-Jar needs no production code change: the shadow plugin came with
add-gradle-support, and A-Gradle already pointed it at goat.Goat and
named its output goat.jar. Verified against the exact usage the
requirement describes -- copy the JAR into an empty folder, open a
command window there, run `java -jar "goat.jar"` -- which works, writes
its data/goat.txt beside the JAR, and reloads that list on the next run.
The manifest carries Main-Class: goat.Goat, written by the application
plugin from build.gradle's mainClass.

What was missing was the instructions, so the README now covers:

- the four wrapper commands (run, test, build, shadowJar), with a note
  that the wrapper fetches Gradle itself so none need it installed;
- the three steps to run the JAR, including why the double quotes are
  there (paths with spaces);
- that data/goat.txt is created in the folder the command was run from,
  which is the reason step 1 says to give the JAR a folder of its own --
  run it somewhere else and you get a different list;
- that the JAR is not committed, because generated binaries do not
  belong in version control, and is published through GitHub releases.

Also fixed a path that went stale in A-Packages: the IntelliJ setup
section still pointed at src/main/java/Goat.java, which moved into the
goat package.

build/libs is already covered by .gitignore, so no JAR can be committed
by accident.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add the missing Javadoc header comments
commitResults.messageBody:
Every public class and most methods carry a header comment already, but
seven declarations do not, and `gradlew javadoc` reports two more.

Let's document them:

- Goat.main had no comment at all, despite being the program's entry
  point. Its @param explains that args is ignored, which is the only
  thing a reader would wonder about.
- The five execute() overrides and ExitCommand.isExit() inherited their
  comment from Command. That is allowed only when the parent's wording
  applies exactly, and here it does not: each command does something
  different, which is the whole point of the hierarchy. Each now uses
  {@inheritDoc} and adds what that command in particular does, plus the
  conditions under which it throws.
- The AddCommand, DeleteCommand and MarkCommand constructors had a
  @param line but no summary sentence, so their documentation began
  mid-thought.
- Task's two protected fields were undocumented. They are not private,
  so a subclass author reads them as part of the API.

ExitCommand.execute() is worth a comment precisely because it is empty:
without one, the next reader has to work out whether that is deliberate.

No behaviour change. `gradlew build` passes and `gradlew javadoc` now
reports only the implicit-default-constructor warnings, which are about
constructors nobody wrote.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a skill for the Java coding standard
commitResults.messageBody:
Java code in this project has no stated standard, so decisions about
naming, layout and imports are made case by case and drift apart.

Let's adopt the SE-EDU Java coding standard (intermediate level) and
capture it as the project skill seedu-java-coding-standard, so the rules
are available to read at the moment code is written rather than looked up
after the fact.

A skill rather than a section of AGENTS.md because the rules are long,
and only matter while a .java file is open. AGENTS.md names the skill and
points to it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a skill for the Git conventions
commitResults.messageBody:
Commit messages in this repository are written to no stated convention.
They are readable, but subject lines run well past 50 characters and the
bodies are not wrapped, which makes them awkward in a terminal log.

Let's adopt the SE-EDU Git conventions and capture them as the project
skill seedu-git-standard, alongside the Java one.

The skill also records how this repository names its increment branches
and tags, since those follow the course materials rather than the
convention's kebab-case rule and that exception is worth writing down.

commitResults.messageTitle: Follow the SE-EDU Java coding standard
commitResults.messageBody:
The code predates the standard adopted in the previous two commits, so
parts of it do not comply.

Let's bring it into line:

- Import blocks in 11 files listed the project's own imports before
  java.* and org.*. The standard fixes the order as static, java, javax,
  org, com, then project, with a blank line between groups.
- Nine comments used British spellings (behaviour, recognised,
  unrecognised) where the standard asks for American.
- StorageTest wrote several class names out in full inline
  (java.util.List.of, new goat.task.Deadline) instead of importing them.
- Parser and DateTimes hold only static methods but had an implicit
  public constructor, so either could be instantiated to no purpose.
  Both now have a documented private one.

Line length, indentation and brace style already comply: nothing exceeds
even the 110-character soft limit, and there are no tabs.

No behavior change. Both the Gradle build and text-ui-test pass.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a find command to search task descriptions
commitResults.messageBody:
A list that only grows is hard to use: once it holds twenty tasks, the
only way to answer "did I add that thing about the book?" is to read the
whole thing.

Let's add "find <keyword>", which shows the tasks whose descriptions
contain the keyword, numbered from 1 within the results.

The search lives on TaskList, not in the command. The list is the thing
being searched, and it is the only class that can walk its own contents;
putting it there also keeps it testable without a Ui or a save file. It
returns a new TaskList rather than a raw list so the matches can be
numbered and shown by the same code that handles the full list. The
returned list is separate but holds the same Task objects, so a match can
still be marked.

Matching is case-insensitive and on a substring, so "book" finds "Book
club" and "port" finds "sports". Both make the search more forgiving,
which suits someone half-remembering a phrase.

Task gains getDescription() so the search reads the description itself
rather than picking it back out of the formatted toString().

Parser rejects a bare "find": a search for nothing would match every
task, which is not what anyone typing it means.

A no-match result says so in words instead of printing an empty header,
so the reply always tells the user something.

Covered by nine TaskList tests, eight FindCommand tests and three Parser
tests, and text-ui-test now runs find with a match, a differently-cased
match, no match, and no keyword.

commitResults.messageTitle: Bring the find command up to the new standards
commitResults.messageBody:
Git merged all three branches without a single textual conflict, and the
build passed afterwards, but the merge is not correct.

The Level-9 branch was cut from master before A-JavaDoc and
A-CodingStandard landed, so the code it adds was written to the older
practice. Nothing in it overlaps textually with what those two branches
changed, so nothing conflicted and nothing complained.

Let's finish the merge by hand:

- FindCommandTest listed its imports in the pre-standard order, with the
  project's own imports ahead of org.*.
- Two of its comments spelled "capitalisation" the British way.
- FindCommand.execute() was the only override left without its own
  header comment, since A-JavaDoc gave one to each of the five that
  existed when that branch was cut.

This is the failure mode worth remembering from this exercise: a merge
that Git reports as clean can still leave the code inconsistent, because
Git compares text and a coding standard is about everything the text
does not say.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add Checkstyle to enforce the coding standard
commitResults.messageBody:
The coding standard adopted in A-CodingStandard lives in prose, in a skill
file. Nothing checks it, so compliance depends on whoever is writing the
code remembering to look. The Level-9 merge showed the cost of that: a
clean merge and a green build still left a new test file with imports in
the wrong order and two British spellings.

Let's add Checkstyle, with the AddressBook Level 3 configuration the
course points to. It runs as part of `check`, so `gradlew build` now
fails on a style violation rather than reporting success.

It found 41 violations, in three groups:

- 32 indentation errors. The config sets caseIndent=4, so a `case` label
  sits one level inside its `switch`. The three switches here had them
  flush with the switch, which is what the prose standard's own example
  shows. The two sources genuinely disagree; the config wins, because it
  is the one that gates the build.
- 7 declaration order errors. A-CodingStandard gave Parser and DateTimes
  private constructors to stop them being instantiated, and put them
  directly under the class declaration, ahead of the constants. The
  expected order is static variables, instance variables, constructors,
  then methods.
- 2 separator wrap errors in ParserTest, where a wrapped line began with
  the `(` of a lambda instead of keeping it on the line before.

None of these was a bug, which is the point: they are exactly the kind of
drift that is invisible in review and tedious to argue about, and the
tool settles them without discussion.

commitResults.messageTitle: Record that Checkstyle arbitrates the standard
commitResults.messageBody:
Two descriptions of the same standard now exist: the prose in the
seedu-java-coding-standard skill, and the rules Checkstyle enforces. They
disagree on how far a `case` label is indented, and they will drift again.

Let's state which one wins. The skill now says the config is
authoritative, on the grounds that it is what fails the build, and
records the caseIndent rule that caused the disagreement.

The skill also notes what Checkstyle cannot see - American spelling, and
whether a Javadoc summary says anything the method name does not already
say - so the prose is not mistaken for redundant now that a tool exists.

AGENTS.md gains the commands for running Checkstyle on its own and where
its reports are written.

Goat only runs in a terminal, which makes it awkward to show anyone and
awkward to use: the reply scrolls away, and there is no way to look back
at the conversation.

Let's add a JavaFX window, alongside the terminal version rather than in
place of it. Both drive the same parser, task list and save file.

The join between them is one method. Goat.getResponse(input) parses one
line, runs it, and returns what the user should see as plain text; the
window puts that in a speech bubble. Ui does the work that makes this
possible: every reply is collected into a buffer as well as shown, so the
terminal version prints as it goes and ignores the buffer, while
Ui.forGui() prints nothing and hands the buffer over. No Command and no
TaskList knows which front end is running.

Two things the GUI has to do that the loop in run() did for free:

- The farewell. run() shows it after its loop ends, so ExitCommand does
  nothing. There is no loop here, so getResponse shows it and sets a flag
  the window reads to know it should close. It waits a moment first, or
  the reply would vanish before it could be read.
- The greeting. The constructor no longer prints it, so the window asks
  for it with getWelcomeMessage() and shows it as the opening bubble.
  A complaint about a damaged save file travels with it.

Launcher exists because Main extends Application, and the JVM refuses to
start such a class directly unless JavaFX was loaded as modules, which it
is not in a fat JAR. Launching from a plain class gets past that check.
This is the mistake the increment specifically warns about.

The build now declares JavaFX for every platform, not just this machine,
so the JAR published as a release runs where it is downloaded. The JDK in
use here bundles JavaFX, which would have hidden the problem.

The window's entry point is goat.gui.Launcher. goat.Goat keeps its own
main() for the terminal version, which text-ui-test runs by class name,
so that suite is untouched and still passes byte for byte.

Verified by opening the window and by running the packaged JAR; 22 new
tests cover getResponse, the exit flag, the greeting, and Ui's buffering.

commitResults.messageTitle: Fix the Mac natives bundled in the JAR
commitResults.messageBody:
The JAR declares JavaFX for five platforms so that it runs wherever it is
downloaded. Two of those five, 'mac' and 'mac-aarch64', ship dylibs with
identical names: libglass.dylib and seven others. A flat JAR holds one
file per name, so one set silently overwrote the other, and the Intel set
won on an Apple Silicon machine.

Nothing reported this. The build succeeded, and running the JAR here
worked, because the JDK in use bundles JavaFX as a named module that
takes precedence over anything on the classpath. The bundled copy was
never exercised, so the wrong natives were never loaded.

Let's drop the Intel Mac classifier. Only one of the two can survive the
merge, and Apple Silicon is the one to keep. Windows and both Linux
architectures are unaffected, since their natives have distinct
extensions and do not collide.

Verified by running the JAR with --limit-modules, which hides the JDK's
own JavaFX and forces the bundled copy to be used: the toolkit starts and
the window opens. The dylibs in the JAR now checksum to the aarch64 ones.

Anyone on an Intel Mac can still run the app with `gradlew run`, which
resolves natives for the machine it is on rather than from the JAR.

commitResults.messageTitle: Follow the tutorial's JavaFX build config
commitResults.messageBody:
The JavaFX dependencies were assembled from what looked reasonable rather
than copied from the tutorial the module points to: JavaFX 25.0.4, with
win, mac-aarch64, linux and linux-aarch64 classifiers, plus a manifest
attribute and a jvmArgs line to quiet some warnings.

Every one of those choices was defensible on its own and none of them
came from the course materials. That is how a build ends up working on
the machine it was written on and nowhere else.

Let's replace the block with the tutorial's, verbatim: JavaFX 17.0.7,
twelve lines covering base, controls, fxml and graphics for win, mac and
linux, and mainClass.set for the entry point. The two invented tweaks are
gone as well, since neither is in the tutorial or the Gradle template the
course supplies, and the manifest one did not work here anyway.

Known consequence, recorded so it is not rediscovered later: the
tutorial's 'mac' classifier is x86_64, so the natives inside the JAR do
not match an Apple Silicon CPU. It does not show up in normal use here,
because this JDK bundles JavaFX as a named module that takes precedence
over anything on the classpath, and `java -jar` therefore never reaches
the bundled copy. Forcing it with --limit-modules fails with an
UnsatisfiedLinkError naming the architecture. Consistency with the
materials is worth more than a private fix for this.

Verified: gradlew build passes, 186 tests pass, text-ui-test passes, and
the window opens from the JAR.

Several assumptions in the code hold by construction rather than by
checking. A reader has to reconstruct the argument each time, and if one
is ever broken by a later change, the symptom appears far from the cause.

Let's state them as assertions. They document the assumption where it is
made, and they fail loudly at the point of breakage when enabled.

Placed at seven points:

- TaskList.toIndex, after the range check, so the conversion cannot
  silently produce an index outside the list.
- TaskList.find, where the result can never be longer than the list
  searched.
- Parser.parse, where parseCommandType throws rather than returning
  nothing, so a command has definitely been recognized by that line.
- Parser.parseNewTask, whose default branch parse() can never reach.
- Goat's constructor, which must leave the chatbot usable whether the
  save file was read, missing or damaged.
- Ui.readCommand, which has no Scanner when built for a GUI.
- Ui.takeResponse, which must leave the buffer empty.

None of these replaces a check on user input. Bad input is a thing users
do and is answered with a message; a failed assertion means the program
itself is wrong.

Assertions are off unless the JVM is given -ea, so build.gradle now
passes it to both the test and run tasks. Without that they would be
dead weight. Verified by breaking the index calculation deliberately:
the test run fails with AssertionError rather than a wrong answer.

commitResults.messageTitle: Remove duplicated knowledge in the code
commitResults.messageBody:
Four things in the code were stated in more than one place. Each pair
must agree for the program to work, and nothing makes them agree.

Let's give each one a single home.

The save file's vocabulary was split across two packages. Todo wrote "T"
and Storage read "T"; the same for "D" and "E", for the " | " separator
in four toFileFormat methods, and for the "1" and "0" done flags. Change
one side and saving still works, loading still works, and a saved list
no longer loads. The letters are now constants on the task classes
themselves, and Storage switches on those, so reading and writing cannot
disagree.

parseTask did two jobs: decide which task a line describes, and apply
its done flag. Those are now buildTask and applyDoneFlag, with a
requireFields helper replacing three near-identical length checks.

Storage indexed its fields by number: parts[0] through parts[4], with a
bare 3 and 5 for the length checks. What parts[3] means depended on the
task type two lines above. Each position is now named.

ListCommand and FindCommand each held the same loop for numbering tasks
under a heading. It is now Command.formatNumbered, which both call.

The save file path was written out in Goat.main and again in the
window's Main, so the two front ends could have opened different files.
It is now Goat.DEFAULT_SAVE_PATH.

No behavior change: the Gradle build passes, 186 tests pass, and
text-ui-test still matches byte for byte, which is the check that
matters most here since the save format was touched.

commitResults.messageTitle: Use streams where they say more than a loop
commitResults.messageBody:
Five places in the code loop over a collection to filter it, map it, or
search it. Each loop mixes what is being computed with the mechanics of
accumulating a result, and the mechanics are the larger half.

Let's rewrite those five as streams, where the operation names itself.

- TaskList.find was six lines, four of them about collecting matches.
  It is now a filter on what counts as a match.
- CommandType.fromKeyword looped over the constants with an early return
  and a throw after the loop. findFirst().orElseThrow says the same in
  one expression, and the throw is no longer separated from the search
  by the loop body.
- Storage.save maps each task to its saved line.
- ListCommand and FindCommand build a heading followed by numbered
  lines. Stream.concat joins the two without an array index to keep in
  step with the loop counter.

Three of these index from 1 with IntStream.rangeClosed rather than
streaming a collection directly, because TaskList deliberately does not
hand out the list it wraps. The stream form keeps that constraint and
still reads as a mapping.

TaskList.get throws a checked exception, which a lambda cannot pass on,
so the three call sites go through a small private helper. Each documents
why the exception cannot happen: the range is derived from the size.

Loops were left alone where they were already clear, notably Storage.load,
which reports the line number of a damaged entry and so needs the index
for its error message rather than only for iteration.

No behavior change: the Gradle build passes, 186 tests pass, and
text-ui-test matches byte for byte.
Add assertions for internal assumptions
Remove duplicated knowledge in the code

A-CodeQuality and A-Streams both rewrote the numbered-list code in
ListCommand and FindCommand, so Git could not merge them and asked for a
decision.

Neither side alone is the right answer:

- A-CodeQuality noticed the two commands held the same loop and pulled it
  into Command.formatNumbered, removing the duplication but keeping the
  loop.
- A-Streams replaced each loop with a stream, saying more clearly what is
  being built but leaving the duplication in place, now in two copies of
  the stream instead of two copies of the loop.

Let's take the call sites from A-CodeQuality and the implementation from
A-Streams: the commands call formatNumbered, and formatNumbered is
written with Stream.concat. The per-command describe helpers A-Streams
added are gone, since the numbering now happens in one place.

Storage merged without help and was checked rather than assumed: it has
A-Streams' mapping in save and A-CodeQuality's named field positions and
task type constants in parseTask.

Resolved locally rather than through the web interface, so the tests
could be run against the result: the Gradle build passes, 186 tests pass,
and text-ui-test matches byte for byte.
Use streams where they say more than a loop

commitResults.messageTitle: Restore the two lost TaskList assertions
commitResults.messageBody:
A-Assertions claims seven assertion points, but only five reached master.
The two in TaskList were lost before that branch was committed, so the
commit message describes work the commit does not contain.

They went missing during the check that assertions actually fire: the
index calculation was broken on purpose, the test run confirmed an
AssertionError, and the file was then restored with
`git checkout -- TaskList.java`. That discards every uncommitted change
to the file, not only the deliberate one, so it took the assertions with
it. The build stayed green because assertions are not what makes it pass.

Let's put them back. toIndex asserts that the index it returns is inside
the list, and find asserts that a result is never longer than the list
searched. The second is written against the streamed find that A-Streams
introduced, since that is what is on master now.

Verified the same way as before, but with the file committed first, so
that reverting the deliberate break could not take anything else with it.
